title: Productivity: Chalmers lifts bank bond caps, deceased estate withdrawal limits
full_text:
Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the government's plan to allow banks to issue more debt will improve competition and productivity in the sector as rising inflation and interest rates sour the economic outlook.
In a speech to the Citi A50 Australian Economic Forum on Friday, Chalmers flagged the release of draft legislation to expand the cap on banks' covered bond issuance, one of the measures initially announced in May's federal budget aimed at reducing financial sector compliance costs by $780 million a year.
Changes to streamline reporting requirements for smaller banks and a doubling in the withdrawal limit on deceased persons' estate-related expenses to $30,000 were also released for consultation on Friday. The Treasurer signalled plans to remake bank regulations due to expire in April to ensure they remained fit for purpose.
"Our sensible proposals will reduce unnecessary costs in the financial sector without compromising on standards," said Chalmers.
The changes come as the Albanese government - and Chalmers in particular - try to counter criticisms about the quality of their economic management, which have grown louder as economists sound the alarm on stagnating productivity levels and climbing interest bills on government debt.
As reported by The Australian Financial Review, the speech also flagged looming downgrades to the government's growth and unemployment forecasts in the mid-year budget update due in December as inflation and borrowing costs climbed around the world.
"Within 10 years [from 2020 to 2030] the number of G20 countries with gross debt above 100 per cent of GDP is expected to almost triple," Chalmers said. "Treasury is in the process of revising all the numbers for the mid-year update. Higher interest rates and higher inflation are likely to mean softer growth and slightly higher unemployment."
Covered bonds are a type of secured debt backed by both the issuer and a designated pool of assets, which came into existence in Australia after the global financial crisis.
Under the plans, authorised deposit-taking institutions will be allowed to increase the proportion of their total assets in Australia used in "cover pools" for these bonds from 8 per cent to 12 per cent.
Debt under these bonds is generally cheaper to issue because it is doubly secured, but banks typically don't issue the full amount allowed under the cap in case they need to raise funds in a pinch.
The changes to bond issuance caps were well received by industry players.
Bank of Queensland chief executive Rod Finch said that in addition to supporting the government's broader productivity agenda, the benefit of the changes would flow through to customers.
"This is a sensible reform and one BoQ has advocated for as it is a step towards levelling the playing field for smaller banks," he said. "Giving banks like BoQ greater access to efficient wholesale funding gives us more capacity to compete, invest and lend, which is ultimately good for customers. "
Australian Banking Association chief executive and former Liberal senator Simon Birmingham also welcomed the changes to bond caps and the changes to reporting rules and regulation.
"Sensible reforms like these cut unnecessary cost without lowering protections for customers," he said.
A review of small and medium-sized banks by the Council of Financial Regulators published in August 2025 found a higher covered bond cap would especially benefit mid-sized banks, who could access funding at a lower cost and for longer terms.
- with James Eyers
